name: aglio e olio
instructions:
The canonical italian oil-and-garlic pasta. Minimum-viable italian pasta — 5 ingredients plus salt and pasta water. Optionally extended with separately-cooked broccoli or green beans (see OPTIONAL VEGETABLE note).

SERVES 2-3 — but MAKE MORE SPAGHETTI THAN YOU THINK (see NOT ENOUGH SPAGHETTI failure mode).

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 1/3 to 1/2 cup good olive oil
- 6-8 cloves garlic, THINLY SLICED (not minced, not mashed — see notes)
- red chili flakes (a generous pinch — non-optional)
- freshly cracked black pepper (non-optional)
- fresh parsley, roughly chopped
- spaghetti or linguine — more than you think you need
- salt (for the pasta water, generous)

OPTIONAL VEGETABLE (cooked separately — steamed or braised):
- broccoli florets, OR
- green beans (trimmed, 1-inch lengths or whole)

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. (If using a vegetable) COOK THE BROCCOLI OR GREEN BEANS SEPARATELY — steam or braise until just tender (bright green, still with bite). Set aside.

2. Boil pasta in well-salted water — USE LESS WATER THAN USUAL (higher pasta-to-water ratio) so the water gets EXTRA STARCHY (see STARCHY WATER note). Cook until just al dente. Reserve a generous cup of pasta water.

3. Meanwhile, warm the olive oil over LOW heat in a wide pan. Add the sliced garlic and red chili flakes. Cook gently until the garlic is fragrant and just barely golden — never brown. Burnt garlic ruins the dish; low and slow is the only technique.

4. ADD THE SPAGHETTI DIRECTLY TO THE HOT OIL — transfer with tongs straight from the pot (dripping pasta water with it) into the garlic oil. Add the cooked vegetable if using, plus a splash more reserved pasta water. Toss vigorously to emulsify the oil and starchy water into a light sauce that clings to the strands.

5. Off heat, fold in the chopped parsley and a generous grind of black pepper. Salt to taste. Scatter whole toasted sunflower seeds on top if using (see notes — never crushed).
notes:
MINIMUM-VIABLE ITALIAN PASTA: the italian pantry-pasta shape at its most minimal — olive oil, garlic, chili, parsley, pasta, salt. Nothing to hide behind, which is the whole point. Every ingredient has to be good, and the technique has to be right.

=== FAILURE MODE — NOT MAKING ENOUGH SPAGHETTI ===

Easy to underestimate how much pasta this dish needs. Unlike a bolognese or any heavy-sauced pasta — where the sauce itself is a big part of what fills you up — aglio e olio has no heavy sauce; the spaghetti IS the meal, and the oil-garlic coating adds flavor but almost no bulk. Portion sizes that would be right for a sauced pasta come up short here. Make more spaghetti than you think you need — err a full serving over your instinct.

=== BURNT GARLIC IS THE #1 TECHNIQUE FAILURE ===

This dish lives or dies on the garlic bloom. Cook it LOW and SLOW in the olive oil — the goal is fragrant, just barely golden garlic. Brown or burnt garlic makes the entire dish taste acrid and there's no rescuing it. If you burn the garlic, throw it out, wipe the pan, start over. This is the single most important technique note.

=== THINLY SLICED GARLIC — NOT MINCED, NOT MASHED ===

Thin slices give you the surface area to release flavor into the oil without going to paste — and they don't burn as fast as minced. Minced garlic goes from raw to burnt in seconds; mashed/crushed garlic disperses into the oil and burns even faster while muddying the texture. Thin slices give a wider window AND stay as distinct sweet-garlic chips in the finished dish.

=== EXTRA-STARCHY PASTA WATER — USE LESS WATER (HIGHER PASTA-TO-WATER RATIO) ===

Aglio e olio has no other emulsifier, so the pasta water's starch concentration is load-bearing. Boil the pasta in DELIBERATELY LESS WATER than usual — a higher pasta-to-water ratio concentrates the released starch, and the extra-starchy water emulsifies with the oil into a sauce that actually clings. Standard big-pot-of-water dilutes the starch too much for this dish. Reserve more than you think you need; toss vigorously to emulsify.

=== ADD THE SPAGHETTI DIRECTLY TO THE HOT OIL ===

Transfer the pasta straight from the pot into the garlic oil with tongs — dripping wet, carrying pasta water with it. Don't drain-in-a-colander-then-add; the colander step loses the clinging starch water and cools the pasta. The direct transfer is what kicks off the emulsification immediately in the hot pan.

=== GENEROUS OLIVE OIL — GOOD QUALITY ===

This is a dish where the olive oil is the sauce, so quality matters. Peppery, grassy, real EVOO — not a neutral cooking oil.

=== OPTIONAL VEGETABLE — BROCCOLI OR GREEN BEANS, COOKED SEPARATELY ===

Broccoli or green beans extend the dish into a fuller meal. COOK THEM SEPARATELY — steamed or braised — then fold in with the pasta at the toss. (Earlier versions blanched the vegetables in the pasta water; walked back — separate cooking gives better control over doneness and keeps the pasta water's starch concentration for the sauce.)

- BROCCOLI: more surface area, more chew per bite; florets catch the garlic oil in their crevices. Reads more rustic.
- GREEN BEANS: stay more discrete — long-and-crunchy against the pasta — read cleaner.
Pick one, not both.

=== CHEESE — NOT CANONICAL, BUT NOT WRONG ===

Aglio e olio traditionally skips cheese — the dish is meant to be a lean oil-and-garlic pasta. Some people grate parmesan or pecorino on top; it's not wrong but it's not the classic form. If you want cheesy pasta, this isn't the recipe to modify — go make something else.

=== SUNFLOWER SEEDS ARE PRIMARY — BUT DON'T CRUSH THEM ===

Toasted sunflower seeds scattered on top add a subtle nutty crunch that pairs cleanly with the garlic oil. Non-negotiable precondition: DO NOT CRUSH THEM. Whole toasted seeds only — never grind them into dust, and never process them with breadcrumbs. Pine nuts tolerate being crushed to dust with breadcrumbs (see pine nut breadcrumbs composite); sunflower seeds do NOT. Crushed sunflower seeds turn the dish CHALKY — a gritty dry-mineral mouthfeel that the light oil-and-pasta base can't hide. Same underlying property as the sunflower-seeds-in-red-pesto clash (see [[sicilian-pesto-rosso]]). Whole seeds, scattered late, no processing.

=== WHERE THIS TURNS INTO PASTA CON LE SARDE (SICILIAN SARDINE PASTA) ===

IF YOU START ADDING FISH, BREADCRUMBS, PINE NUTS, RAISINS, LEMON, AND/OR TOMATO — YOU'RE MAKING SARDINE PASTA: aglio e olio and pasta con le sarde share the same starting point (oil + garlic + chili + long pasta) but they diverge quickly. Once you add ANY of the following, you're on the sardine-pasta branch, not aglio e olio anymore:
- CANNED SARDINES or ANCHOVIES
- TOASTED BREADCRUMBS (topping)
- PINE NUTS
- RAISINS
- LEMON (juice or zest)
- FRESH TOMATOES
- FENNEL BULB or FENNEL SEEDS (whole, textural)
Note that FENNEL POWDER (ground) is welcome in the aglio e olio base itself — a small pinch adds background anise depth without pushing the dish into sardine territory. It's the whole-fennel forms (bulb, seeds) that carry the sicilian sardine signature.
Sardine pasta is the more complicated expression — it's got the same DNA but with layered sicilian sweet-sour-salty character. See sardine-parsley-pasta for that recipe. Don't try to combine — if you're reaching for the sardines and pine nuts, commit to that dish; if you want the clean oil-and-garlic register, keep this one lean.
